subject: Engineering Fundamentals
title: Composites in Aerospace: Lighter, Stronger, Smarter
description: A quick, practical guide to Composites in Aerospace: Lighter, Stronger, Smarter.

hook.text: The Boeing 787 Dreamliner is 50% composite material by weight. Aluminum aircraft are becoming the exception, not the rule.

buildup.text: Carbon fiber reinforced polymer is stronger than steel at one-fifth the weight. Carbon fiber layers are bonded with epoxy resin.

discovery.text: Composites don't corrode like aluminum. The 787 flies with higher cabin humidity, reducing passenger fatigue on long flights.

twist.text: Composite damage is hard to spot. A dropped tool causes internal delamination invisible from the surface. Ultrasonic scans help.

climax.text: Self-healing composites embed resin microcapsules that break when cracked. They seal damage automatically — like living tissue.

punchline.text: Lighter than metal. Stronger than steel. Harder to inspect than both.

quiz.question: What is a key disadvantage of composite materials in aircraft?
options: Composites weaken dramatically at high altitudes due to UV radiation
Internal damage like delamination can be invisible from the surface, requiring special scans
Carbon fiber becomes brittle in cold temperatures encountered at cruising altitude
